passages.title: Campaigns and remaining peoples
passages.summary: Judah and other tribes fight local campaigns. Caleb, Othniel, and Achsah reappear. Many Canaanite populations remain.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: Which tribes drive out their neighbors? Which leave them in place or force them to work?

contextNote.title: Remaining peoples complicate the conquest account
contextNote.text: The notices repeatedly distinguish possession from complete removal. Some tribes impose forced labor instead. These details prepare the book's conflicts within a land already called Israel's inheritance.

passages.title: The recurring cycle
passages.summary: An angel rebukes Israel. Joshua’s generation dies. Later generations serve other gods, face enemies, and receive deliverers.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies repentance and the Lord’s repeated willingness to receive people who return.

contextNote.title: A generation change becomes a problem of memory
contextNote.text: The new generation lacks the earlier generation's knowledge. The book then presents repeated rescue without lasting change. Deliverance can interrupt suffering while failing to produce continued faithfulness.

passages.title: Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar
passages.summary: Othniel defeats Cushan-rishathaim. Ehud kills Eglon and leads a revolt against Moab. A short notice records Shamgar’s victory.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The older Church manual studies Israel's return to God during trouble.

contextNote.title: Deliverance uses an unexpected advantage
contextNote.text: Ehud conceals his weapon and later draws it with his left hand. The account links bodily difference with access to the ruler. Its violent reversal challenges the assumption that power rests only with the stronger army.

passages.title: Deborah, Barak, and Jael
passages.summary: Deborah calls Barak against Sisera. The army defeats Sisera’s force near Kishon. Jael kills the fleeing commander.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Deborah’s influence and asks how faith can help other people act.

contextNote.title: Victory disrupts expected roles
contextNote.text: Barak asks Deborah to go with him. The promised victory then gives its final honor to another woman. Jael acts outside the formal army. Read chapter 5’s song beside chapter 4’s prose account. Their different forms show how a community tells and celebrates the same victory.

passages.title: The song of Deborah
passages.summary: Deborah and Barak sing about the battle. They praise willing tribes and Jael. Sisera’s mother waits for him to return.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The older manual studies willing service and courage. Read the poem’s celebration beside its depiction of harm.

contextNote.title: A victory song also judges participation
contextNote.text: The song names tribes that joined and those that stayed away. Praise therefore becomes a public account of shared duty. Its final household scene connects battlefield victory with another family's waiting and loss.

passages.title: Gideon’s call
passages.summary: Gideon receives a call during Midianite raids. He destroys his father’s altar and asks for signs with a fleece.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies trust when God’s instructions differ from what a person expects.

contextNote.title: The first conflict occurs inside Gideon's household
contextNote.text: Destroying the altar brings threats from Gideon's own town. His father answers those threats rather than defending the shrine. The rescue story first tests inherited worship before confronting the outside raiders.

passages.title: Gideon’s reduced force
passages.summary: Gideon’s army is reduced to three hundred. A dream encourages him. Trumpets, jars, and torches precede the enemy’s flight.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies reliance on God. Consider how confidence changes when ordinary advantages are removed.

contextNote.title: Reduced numbers change the explanation of victory
contextNote.text: The army's reduction prevents the people from claiming independent success. The remaining men's noise and light create confusion rather than a conventional attack. The form of victory matters to the account's stated purpose.

passages.title: Victory, revenge, and the ephod
passages.summary: Gideon pursues Zebah and Zalmunna, punishes towns that refused help, and kills the kings. He rejects kingship but makes an ephod.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies trust. The older manual also warns about the ephod and acknowledges the account’s change after victory.

contextNote.title: A deliverer's achievement can produce another danger
contextNote.text: Gideon rejects the title of king but collects gold from victory. The resulting worship object becomes a trap for his household. His words and his lasting influence point in different directions.

passages.title: Abimelech and Jotham’s warning
passages.summary: Abimelech kills his brothers and becomes king at Shechem. Jotham warns through a tree fable. Civil conflict ends with Abimelech’s death.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The manual studies Jotham’s warning. How does Abimelech’s violence help explain the warning about the thorn bush?

contextNote.title: The tree story examines consent to dangerous rule
contextNote.text: Jotham's fable gives the least useful plant the royal position. Its promised shelter comes with a threat of fire. The later conflict makes that warning part of the account's political judgment.

passages.title: Tola, Jair, and renewed distress
passages.summary: Brief notices record Tola and Jair. Israel serves several gods and faces Philistine and Ammonite pressure. The people confess and remove foreign gods.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The manual studies the return to God. Consider the actions that make a stated change visible.

contextNote.title: Confession cannot function as a quick transaction
contextNote.text: The first appeal receives a refusal rather than immediate rescue. The people then remove their foreign gods. The sequence distinguishes words of distress from changed shared practice.

passages.title: Jephthah and his daughter
passages.summary: Gilead’s elders recall the expelled Jephthah to fight Ammon. He makes a vow. His only daughter greets him after victory.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The older manual reads the vow as lifelong service. Hayes reads it as sacrifice. The readings differ over the daughter’s fate.

contextNote.title: A vow can expose failed judgment
contextNote.text: Jephthah’s vow makes his daughter bear the cost of his success. The story gives her grief and her companions space. No command from God requires this vow. The account does not make every action of a deliverer a model. Deliverance in war can exist beside failure within a household.

passages.title: Conflict at the river
passages.summary: Jephthah’s men fight Ephraim and use pronunciation at Jordan crossings to identify fugitives. Short notices record Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The manual compares the conflict with Gideon’s earlier response. Consider how an insult can become collective harm.

contextNote.title: A speech difference becomes a weapon
contextNote.text: The crossing guards use pronunciation to identify people seeking escape. An ordinary difference in speech becomes grounds for killing. The rescue cycle now includes deadly division between Israel's own groups.

passages.title: Samson’s birth announced
passages.summary: An angel visits Manoah’s wife and later Manoah. The child is to be a Nazirite. Samson is born and begins to receive the Spirit.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies covenant faithfulness. The manual treats the angel as God’s messenger rather than naming him as Christ.

contextNote.title: The mother interprets the encounter more clearly
contextNote.text: Manoah fears death after the encounter. His wife reasons from the gifts and promise they received. Before Samson's birth, the account gives her judgment a leading place.

passages.title: The wedding and the riddle
passages.summary: Samson seeks a woman from Timnah. He kills a lion and proposes a riddle. Threats force his wife to obtain its answer.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies Samson’s choices. How do threats against his wife affect what she does?

contextNote.title: A contest exposes someone with less power
contextNote.text: The wedding guests threaten Samson's wife to obtain the answer. Samson treats the answer as a stolen advantage. Her danger shows the human cost hidden beneath the competition.

passages.title: Retaliation at Lehi
passages.summary: Samson’s wife is given to another man. He burns crops. The Philistines burn her household. Samson’s retaliation continues at Lehi.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The older Church manual studies Samson's strength and his request for water.

contextNote.title: Retaliation spreads beyond its original dispute
contextNote.text: The conflict begins with a marriage grievance and reaches crops and households. Each attack produces another response. The chapter makes victory inseparable from widening damage.

passages.title: Delilah and Samson’s final act
passages.summary: Samson visits Gaza. Delilah receives payment to discover his weakness. He is captured and blinded, then destroys the temple during a gathering.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies covenant faithfulness. The older manual distinguishes Samson’s gift of strength from consistent moral conduct.

contextNote.title: The final victory comes after loss of control
contextNote.text: Samson's earlier strength contrasts with blindness, captivity, and forced work. His final prayer acknowledges dependence rather than unlimited personal power. The closing death toll preserves the violence within that deliverance.

passages.title: Micah’s household shrine
passages.summary: Micah returns stolen silver to his mother. Images are made for a shrine. He hires a traveling Levite as priest.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The manual reads this episode as part of religious decline. Consider the difference between a sacred object and faithful conduct.

contextNote.title: Religious hiring becomes a claim to security
contextNote.text: Micah believes employing a Levite will ensure divine favor. His conclusion treats sacred service as something his household can acquire. The next chapter tests how secure that purchased arrangement really is.

passages.title: The Danite migration
passages.summary: Danite scouts consult Micah’s priest. Armed men take the shrine objects and priest, then attack Laish and rename it Dan.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The older manual places the migration in the book’s closing decline. Read the inhabitants’ loss beside the migrants’ claim.

contextNote.title: Migration carries theft into a new sanctuary
contextNote.text: The armed group takes objects and a priest from Micah. Its new worship center rests on that seizure. The account places sacred claims beside the force used to establish them.

passages.title: The woman at Gibeah
passages.summary: A Levite retrieves his concubine from Bethlehem. At Gibeah, men threaten the guest. The woman is handed over and violently abused.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The older Church manual describes the harm caused by Israel's loss of moral care.

contextNote.title: The final violence reaches inside Israel
contextNote.text: The closing chapters move from foreign enemies to harm within Israel. A woman’s body becomes part of a public call to action. The resulting war brings more loss and further abuse. Repeated statements about Israel having no king frame this breakdown. The book makes readers face the cost of failed public order.

passages.title: War against Benjamin
passages.summary: The tribes gather at Mizpah after hearing the Levite’s report. Benjamin refuses their demand. Repeated battles bring mass death and destruction.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The manual describes the near destruction of Benjamin. Consider how a partial account can influence a community’s judgment.

contextNote.title: The assembly acts on a selective report
contextNote.text: The Levite's speech does not describe his own role in handing over the woman. His report still drives the assembly's decision. Read his account beside chapter 19 before accepting it as the whole event.

passages.title: Women taken and the closing refrain
passages.summary: The assembly regrets Benjamin’s losses. It attacks Jabesh-gilead and arranges the seizure of women at Shiloh.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named localities and approximate regions. They do not establish exact battle sites, ancient roads, or tribal boundaries.

lds.text: The older Church manual condemns the seizure of women as wives.

contextNote.title: A proposed repair repeats harm against women
contextNote.text: The assembly seeks wives after almost destroying Benjamin. Its solutions take women from other communities without their consent. The ending makes failed public judgment extend beyond the battlefield.

events.detail: The closing chapters move from foreign enemies to harm within Israel. A woman’s body becomes part of a public call to action. The resulting war brings more loss and further abuse. Repeated statements about Israel having no king frame this breakdown. The book makes readers face the cost of failed public order.

events.title: War against Benjamin
events.summary: The tribes gather at Mizpah after hearing the Levite’s report. Benjamin refuses their demand. Repeated battles bring mass death and destruction.
events.detail: The Levite's speech does not describe his own role in handing over the woman. His report still drives the assembly's decision. Read his account beside chapter 19 before accepting it as the whole event.

lds.text: The manual describes the near destruction of Benjamin. Consider how a partial account can influence a community’s judgment.

events.title: Women taken and the closing refrain
events.summary: The assembly regrets Benjamin’s losses. It attacks Jabesh-gilead and arranges the seizure of women at Shiloh.
events.detail: The assembly seeks wives after almost destroying Benjamin. Its solutions take women from other communities without their consent. The ending makes failed public judgment extend beyond the battlefield.

guides.title: Judges: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Victory disrupts expected roles
steps.text: Barak asks Deborah to go with him. The promised victory then gives its final honor to another woman. Jael acts outside the formal army. Read chapter 5’s song beside chapter 4’s prose account. Their different forms show how a community tells and celebrates the same victory.

steps.title: A vow can expose failed judgment
steps.text: Jephthah’s vow makes his daughter bear the cost of his success. The story gives her grief and her companions space. No command from God requires this vow. The account does not make every action of a deliverer a model. Deliverance in war can exist beside failure within a household.

steps.title: The final violence reaches inside Israel
steps.text: The closing chapters move from foreign enemies to harm within Israel. A woman’s body becomes part of a public call to action. The resulting war brings more loss and further abuse. Repeated statements about Israel having no king frame this breakdown. The book makes readers face the cost of failed public order.
